gaps: assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-finite-probability-C008: Grinstead and Snell Definition 1.4 (p. 28), with the odds discussion on pp. 27-28, defines odds in favour of E as a ratio r : s of which only r/s matters, gives the converse conversion p = r/(r + s) from stated odds, and reads odds as the rate of a bet a person is willing to make (2 to 1 odds giving probability 2/3). The entry defines only the number P(G)/(1 - P(G)) for P(G) < 1. The ratio convention, the general converse conversion and the source's betting reading of odds are not given for this entry, and the route states them nowhere in general (only isolated instances occur in other sources' chapters, such as Carnap's equitable odds of one to five for probability 1/6).

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-finite-probability-C013: Grinstead and Snell's counterpart Example 4.17 (p. 147), a test for a rare cancer with prior .001, P(+ | cancer) = .99 and P(- | no cancer) = .95, giving posterior .019 so that 98.1 percent of positive results are false positives, ends with an empirical claim: when a group of second-year medical students was asked this question, over half guessed a probability greater than .5. The source gives the task (this question) and the population (a group of second-year medical students) but no design, sample size or uncertainty. Neither the source example nor this claim is presented on the route; the entry substitutes a stipulated model whose weights it declares are not measured data, and it does not record the source's finding together with its missing design and uncertainty; the empirical treatment of base-rate neglect in Part 19 (Gigerenzer and Hoffrage) does not record this source's claim either.

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-integration-expectation-C006: Durrett's 'Notation for special cases' (pp. 23-24) adopts (a) the integral of f(x) dx for Lebesgue measure on R^d and (b) the integral from a to b of f(x) dx for E = [a, b]. Neither convention is defined on the route, although later route entries write Lebesgue integrals that way (for example m(y) as the integral of f(x, y) dx in thm:p15-conditional-density-formulas, and the dx integrals in the Radon-Nikodym annex). Cases (c) dG and (d) counting-measure sums are supplied elsewhere (def:p15-convolution-law, thm:p15-expectation-law-integral).

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-integration-expectation-C016: Durrett titles Theorem 1.6.9 the 'change of variables formula' and explains the name in the Remark that follows: writing h for X and P o h^{-1} for mu gives the integral of f(h(omega)) dP equal to the integral of f(y) d(P o h^{-1}). The entry states and proves the result without the source's name or that explanation, and the name is not recorded for this result elsewhere on the route.

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-measurable-probability-C010: Durrett Example 1.3.2 (p. 15) gives the open rays {(-infinity, x) : x rational} as a generating class for the Borel sets of R, and Example 1.3.3 gives the open rectangles with arbitrary real endpoints for R^d. The theorem states closed rational rays, closed real rays and rational open rectangles only; the open-ray generator, with its measurability test {X < q}, and the real-endpoint rectangle class are not supplied on the route.

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-measurable-probability-C016: Durrett (p. 17) defines an extended random variable as a map from a measurable domain D in F into [-infinity, infinity] carrying the Borel sets of its usual topology, generated by intervals [-infinity, a), (a, b) and (b, infinity]. The entry requires maps defined on all of Omega (def:p15-measurable-map: all functions are defined on all of Omega) and uses the sigma-algebra generated by the sets [-infinity, a], without recording the source's partial-domain variant and without showing that the two sigma-algebras on the extended line coincide. The source variant is narrowed without declaration.

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-measurable-probability-C021: Durrett's Theorem A.1.5 (app. A.1, pp. 457-458) proves that two measures, defined on sigma-fields containing sigma(P), that agree on a pi-system P containing sets A_n increasing to Omega with finite measure, agree on sigma(P). The entry states uniqueness only for probability measures, and the route's sigma-finite uniqueness (thm:p15-premeasure-extension) requires agreement on an algebra. The source's general pi-system uniqueness theorem for sigma-finite measures is not supplied. Durrett also attributes the pi-lambda theorem to Dynkin ('Dynkin's pi-lambda theorem', p. 456); that attribution is not recorded for this theorem on the route (later annexes only use the phrase 'Dynkin system').

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-measure-extension-C007: Durrett (p. 3) justifies the endpoint convention of the intervals (a, b]: closed on the right because b_n decreasing to b gives the intersection of the (a, b_n] equal to (a, b], matching right continuity of F, and open on the left so that complements are finite disjoint unions of members of the semialgebra. assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-regular-conditional-laws-C005: Durrett (p. 214) introduces the nice-space theorem by recording that regular conditional distributions do not always exist, attributes the first example to Dieudonne (1948) with references to Doob (1953, p. 624) and Faden (1985), and explains the obstruction: for each disjoint sequence the countable additivity of P(X in . | G) holds only almost surely, so over many such sequences the exceptional sets may pile up. On the route only the bare nonexistence statement appears (def:p15-w02b-p15-008-limits, item 3); the attribution and the explanation of why a hypothesis on (S, S) is needed are not supplied.

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-regular-conditional-laws-C011: Durrett's Example 4.1.8 (p. 210) is titled 'Borel's paradox' and states the paradox and its resolution: at first glance, for a uniform point on the globe, the longitude and the angle on the great circle should both be uniform; the longitude is, the angle is not, and the paradox evaporates once one sees that the angle is independent of the longitude, so its conditional law is its unconditional law, which is not uniform because there is more area near the equator than near the pole. The entry computes the coordinate laws and the nonuniform conditional law, but it neither names the example nor states the paradox and its resolution; the later phrase 'the Borel paradox' in bayes-factor-computation is not tied to this example.

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-measure-extension-C007: Durrett (p. 3) justifies the endpoint convention of the intervals (a, b]: closed on the right because b_n decreasing to b gives the intersection of the (a, b_n] equal to (a, b], matching right continuity of F, and open on the left so that complements are finite disjoint unions of members of the semialgebra. The entry fixes the half-open convention and its extended endpoint values but supplies neither justification, and neither is stated elsewhere on the route.

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-measure-extension-C012: Durrett's remark after Theorem 1.2.2 (p. 11) states that the scheme of its proof is used to generate random variables on a computer: standard algorithms produce a uniform U, and F^{-1}(U) then has distribution function F. The entry proves that Q_F on the uniform space has law mu_F, but this applied claim is not supplied for the entry or elsewhere on the route.

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-regular-conditional-laws-C005: Durrett (p. 214) introduces the nice-space theorem by recording that regular conditional distributions do not always exist, attributes the first example to Dieudonne (1948) with references to Doob (1953, p. 624) and Faden (1985), and explains the obstruction: for each disjoint sequence the countable additivity of P(X in . | G) holds only almost surely, so over many such sequences the exceptional sets may pile up. On the route only the bare nonexistence statement appears (def:p15-w02b-p15-008-limits, item 3); the attribution and the explanation of why a hypothesis on (S, S) is needed are not supplied.

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-regular-conditional-laws-C011: Durrett's Example 4.1.8 (p. 210) is titled 'Borel's paradox' and states the paradox and its resolution: at first glance, for a uniform point on the globe, the longitude and the angle on the great circle should both be uniform; the longitude is, the angle is not, and the paradox evaporates once one sees that the angle is independent of the longitude, so its conditional law is its unconditional law, which is not uniform because there is more area near the equator than near the pole. The entry computes the coordinate laws and the nonuniform conditional law, but it neither names the example nor states the paradox and its resolution; the later phrase 'the Borel paradox' in bayes-factor-computation is not tied to this example.

Durrett (sec. 1.2, p. 10) remarks that analysts call the indicator 1_A the characteristic function of A, whereas in probability that term is used for something quite different (Section 3.3). The entry (parts lines 280-289) defines indicators without this warning, and it appears nowhere on the P15 route, although the handbook later uses 'characteristic function' for E exp(itX). Supply the remark.

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-measurable-probability-C016: Narrowed source variant. Durrett (sec. 1.3, p. 17) defines an extended random variable as a function whose DOMAIN IS A SET D IN F, with values in [-inf,inf], measurable for the Borel sets of the extended line under its usual topology (generated by [-inf,a), (a,b), (b,inf]). The entry (parts lines 302-321, with line 237) admits only maps defined on all of Omega and equips the extended line with sigma([-inf,a], a real) without identifying this sigma-algebra with those topological Borel sets (no proof of the identification on the route). Durrett's notion of almost-sure convergence (pp. 16-17: X_n converges a.s. when Omega_0 = {lim_n X_n exists} has probability one, the limit then taken as limsup X_n and possibly infinite; this is almost-everywhere convergence of measure theory) is replaced by convergence to a specified real random variable only. Supply the domain-D variant, the identification of the extended sigma-algebra with proof, and the source's a.s.-convergence notion.

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-measurable-probability-C017: Claim of the source omitted. MP-0: thm:p15-w02c-p15-014-probability-mean (Durrett 4.6.3 at p=1, with the extension proved in the annex):
(1) Given convergence in probability, L^p convergence holds iff some tail of |X_n-X|^p is integrable and uniformly integrable. Both directions are proved.
(2) If X_n is in L^p for every n, L^p convergence holds iff (|X_n|^p) is uniformly integrable, and then X is in L^p.

(4) The condition is sufficient but not necessary: X_n=X=Y_p, and X_1=Y_p with X_n=0 for n>=2.

open_components.gap: assessment_dispute: ED26-BM-RAT2021-4-3-C02: Most definitions, theorems and lemmas of the chapter are reconstructed with written proofs, but parts of the source's own definitions and argument are missing. (1) Def. 9 (p. 270) asserts that ordinal equivalence holds iff T' = f(T) for some isotonic f; rationality-4-3.tex lines 291-293 state only that strictly increasing transforms preserve rankings, and the converse (ordinal equivalence yields one global isotonic f) is neither stated nor proved. (2) Def. 8(a) (p. 269) requires the value range of a relevance measure to be a subinterval, proper or improper, of the extended reals; lines 172-180 omit this clause. (3) The p. 268 motivation for the signpost notation, that for mutually relevant A and B, A may be more relevant to B than B is to A under one measure, less under another and equally under a third, is not presented or realized (lines 164-170; thm:p15-r43-measures shows only that D and L agree in direction and that Q is symmetric). (4) Linda (p. 273): the bridge of the argument, that E was designed to be representative of F and unrepresentative of B and that many probabilists explicate the representativeness of a property as the relevance of 'Linda is Phi' to E, is dropped; lines 485-489 reduce it to 'He treats that description as favoring feminist activity and disfavoring bank-teller work'. (5) Raven (p. 272): the source's statement of the problem (a plausible deductivist criterion requires the logical equivalents H and G to be supported alike, so B, and with mild further assumptions C, should support H, which is counterintuitive) and its claim that the negligible positive increment explains the pretheoretical intuition that B, and C, are irrelevant to H are not given (lines 398-425).

assessment_dispute: ED26-BM-RAT2021-4-3-C03: (1) Linda (p. 273): the historical claim that the conjunction fallacy arose most famously in this late-1970s example, the empirical report that a surprisingly large proportion of respondents ranked BF above B (contravening P(BF|E) <= P(B|E)), and the design claim that E was built to be representative of F and unrepresentative of B are omitted; rationality-4-3.tex lines 479-509 give the task and the description but not the reported response pattern, so that empirical claim is not retained with its (unstated) population, design and uncertainty boundaries. (2) The claim-kind inventory def:p15-w02b-p15-024-claim-kinds (inductive-logic-and-confirmation-w02b-p15-024.tex lines 51-59) says the chapter contains three empirical claims; the chapter makes others, e.g. the Linda response proportion, the evidence that delta-p explicates participants' relevance assessments (p. 273), that relevance theory is popular in linguistics and conjectures relevance maximization as a principle of cognition and communication (p. 273), that D, Q and L are the oldest and most commonly used measures (p. 269), that LL is widely used in statistics (p. 270), and that many will balk at the symmetry of Q (p. 272). (3) Omitted normative or justificatory claims: p. 272 'Intuitions on amount symmetry are strong only in the case of asymmetric extreme positivity'; Q's symmetry in the 15/3 example 'which many will balk at, because it ignores the entailment asymmetry'; extreme valuation 'pleases anyone to whom conclusive argument is the strongest argument'; the homomorphism paragraph (structure-preserving maps essential to the predictability of ordinal and quantitative relevance properties of logical complexes; most conditional homomorphisms not practically useful, not all desirable); p. 273 conclusion 'one should seek out such independencies in one's domain of application'; p. 265 that the same relations obtain between statements about past events and between possible experimental results and timeless hypotheses, that 'speaking for' means being evidence for in the diction of jurisprudence and science, and that the informal idea remains vague and prone to apparent exceptions. (4) Note 15 ('(3) is an inessential embellishment that makes things vivid') is cited at line 425 but not presented, and the editorial note (Merin died on 24 May 2019; final minor revisions were made by the editors) is not recorded.

assessment_dispute: ED26-BM-RAT2021-4-3-C05: The finite dependent-source set is fixed (33 references and 7 handbook chapters, def:p15-w02b-p15-024-dependents, inductive-logic-and-confirmation-w02b-p15-024.tex lines 947-1032) and every numbered theorem and lemma has written proofs, but not every promised proof or evidence claim is accounted for: (1) the Def. 9 equivalence of ordinal equivalence with isotonic transformation (p. 270) is given in one direction only (rationality-4-3.tex lines 291-293); (2) the p. 268 claim that the direction comparison for one pair can be greater under one measure, smaller under another and equal under a third is neither realized nor given a standing; (3) the chapter's empirical report on the Linda task (p. 273) and its attribution to many probabilists of the representativeness-as-relevance explication are not recorded, and the empirical-claim inventory (inductive-logic-and-confirmation-w02b-p15-024.tex lines 51-59) counts only three empirical claims, so these claims have no stated standing.

assessment_dispute: ED26-P16-CH-finite-abduction-C001: The entry's definitions, hypotheses and worked boundaries are present (finite-abduction.tex lines 21-48; consistent-theory variant lines 13-16; truth constant and biconditional lines 40-41 with annex lines 35-49; P_empty and P_permitted), but the source's own qualification of the atomic-hypothesis convention is not preserved. Eiter and Gottlob (manuscript p. 10, after Def. 2.2) state that admitting only positive atoms in solutions 'is no restriction of generality, since we may add to T a formula x' <-> F where x' is a new variable that we add to the hypotheses H'. The handbook states the restriction (lines 35-37) and lists 'general formula hypotheses and their translations' as needing a separate treatment (lines 335-338), without the source's no-loss-of-generality claim or its translation. The source's reasons for not requiring H and M disjoint (a manifestation may explain another manifestation) or H union M = V (assumption-based explanations, focusing attention) are also not given; lines 34-35 state only the non-requirements.

assessment_dispute: ED26-P16-CH-finite-abduction-C012: The warning states its boundary (the arrows are material implications; the input has no causal relation, intervention semantics, temporal order or probability; fewer or non-redundant assumptions do not supply causal structure) and points to the separate treatments (finite-abduction.tex lines 326-354), but no boundary case is worked: neither the entry nor the six inputs exhibit an explanation, minimal or minimum-cardinality, whose causal reading the formulas leave undetermined (the P_sizes countervaluation of thm:p16-abduction-truth-boundary is not connected to the causal claim). open_components.gap: assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-systematic-power-C001 partial: the source's example languages are not on the route (Hempel-Oppenheim 1948 pp. 166, 168, n. 36). Missing: L1 (constant a, unary P and Q; two atoms; its four minimal and four maximal sentences listed); L2 (adds b and a binary R; eight atoms, 256 minimal sentences, the source's sample minimal sentence); and the source's description of a maximal sentence as the dual (Church) of a minimal sentence. def:p15-power-language (systematic-power.tex 24-59) gives only the general construction. Text for these items exists only in the unrouted owner file handbook/parts/p15/inductive-logic-and-confirmation-w02c-p15-028.tex (owned by w02c-p15-028), which was not counted.

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-systematic-power-C002 partial: missing from the route (pp. 166, 168-169, n. 37): the L1 minimal and maximal normal forms of P(a), Q(a), P(a)>Q(a), a formally true sentence and a formally false sentence; the 128-member L2 minimal normal forms of P(a) and Q(a); the illustration m_U = 2,1,0,4 (m = 4) of m_U + l_U = m; the source's remark that P(a)vQ(a) has the consequence (Ex)(P(x)vQ(x)), which is neither singular nor formally true; content exclusivity in the source's form (no shared non-formally-true consequence of any form); and the source's justification that the minimal normal form indicates content and the maximal normal form indicates range, listing the possible states of the world that make a sentence true. thm:p15-power-normal-forms states only the general theorem for singular consequences.

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-systematic-power-C003 partial: missing (pp. 164-165, n. 33): the convention that every singular sentence of L expresses a potential datum, so K is a finite class of singular sentences; note 33's statements that data cover actual as well as potential data, that the convention is plausible when the primitives express directly observable attributes, and that this observability assumption is not essential to the formal theory of sections 8-9; the stated reason for letting T be any sentence (generality and simplicity); and the rationale that systematic power is the ratio of the information derivable by means of T to the initial information required.

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-systematic-power-C010 partial: missing (p. 173, n. 41): the source's verdict that the measure-based generalization (the dual counterpart of logical probability) yields a simpler and more comprehensive theory than the section-8 definition; its claim that both versions are purely formal, so that any significant application needs problems about the logical structure and interpretation of the language of science solved; and the investigations by Goodman ([Query], [Counterfactuals], [Infirmities]) and Carnap ([Application]) that it cites for those difficulties.

assessment_dispute: ED26-P15-CH-systematic-power-C016 partial: missing (pp. 170-171, nn. 39-40): the source's claim that Carnap showed the uniform r1 gives p1 characteristics incompatible with the intended meaning of logical probability, which is why alternative range measures were proposed. Also missing is note 40 on the Helmer-Hempel-Oppenheim r_I and dc: r_I is fixed only relative to a sentence I of empirical information; dc is undefined in certain cases with generalized S (McKinsey) and fails some theorems of elementary probability theory; dc has methodologically desirable features; and a systematic-power concept built from r_I is suggested but not pursued. thm:p15-power-weight-choice instead disclaims any link to Carnap's measure.

assessment_dispute: ED26-BM-RAT2021-4-3-C02 partial: Definition 8(a)'s clause that a relevance measure's value range is a subinterval, proper or improper, of the extended reals (Merin 2021 p. 269) is left out of the reconstruction of Transparency (rationality-4-3.tex 172-180).

assessment_dispute: ED26-BM-RAT2021-4-3-C02 partial: the representativeness step of the Linda argument (p. 273) is omitted. In the source, E was designed to be 'representative' of F and 'unrepresentative' of B, and probabilists explicate the representativeness of a property Phi as the relevance of 'Linda is Phi' to E, with F positive and B negative to E. The handbook's model (rationality-4-3.tex 483-500) measures relevance from E to the target and does not state the source's direction.

assessment_dispute: ED26-BM-RAT2021-4-3-C02 partial: the raven argument (pp. 271-272) is not reconstructed in full. Missing: the source's statement of the paradox, in which a deductivist criterion treats the logical equivalents H and G alike, so that B (and, with mild further assumptions, C) would support H, which is counterintuitive; the source's step (3), that G is entailed and thereby supported by C ('a is a white shoe', n. 15), which rationality-4-3.tex 419-423 corrects without reporting; and the source's conclusion that B's merely negligible positive relevance explains the intuition that B, and C, are irrelevant to H.

assessment_dispute: ED26-BM-RAT2021-4-3-C03 partial: the source's Linda report (p. 273) is not stated as a historical and empirical claim with its task, population, design and uncertainty. The report: the example dates from the late 1970s and was presented on an instruction sheet, and a surprisingly large proportion of respondents ranked BF above B, against P(BF|E) <= P(B|E). The handbook gives only the ranking task. In addition, the source's claim that there is evidence that delta-p = P(H|E) - P(H|~E) explicates participants' relevance assessments (Skovgaard-Olsen, Singmann and Klauer 2016b) is weakened to 'research including delta-p' (rationality-4-3.tex 513-521).

assessment_dispute: ED26-BM-RAT2021-4-3-C03 partial: several evaluative, descriptive and scope claims are omitted. From p. 272: extreme valuation 'pleases anyone to whom conclusive argument is the strongest argument'; intuitions on amount symmetry are strong only for asymmetric extreme positivity, and Q's equal values in the divisibility example are something 'many will balk at, because it ignores the entailment asymmetry'; and the section 5.6 framing of conditional operation homomorphisms. From p. 265: the same relevance relations hold between statements about past events, and between experimental results and timeless hypotheses; and the summary calls the task-relative ordinal-equivalence conditions and the disjunctive-evidence properties two extensions of the state of the art.
